CausalChain: Circadian rhythm disruption -> altered hepatic PPARβ/δ activation -> decreased synthesis of PC (18:0/18:1) -> reduced secretion of PC into circulation -> insufficient activation of muscle PPARα -> diminished fatty acid uptake and oxidation in muscle -> systemic dyslipidemia and metabolic impairment
Hypothesis: Modulating the diurnal activity of hepatic PPARβ/δ to restore optimal production and secretion of PC (18:0/18:1) will enhance muscle PPARα-mediated fatty acid oxidation, thereby improving systemic lipid metabolism and insulin sensitivity to counteract metabolic disorders such as NAFLD.
Abstract: Recent research on hepatic PPAR functions has underscored the importance of cell‐specific roles and inter‐organ communication in regulating lipid metabolism. Building on studies that show hepatic PPARβ/δ enhances the synthesis of specific phosphatidylcholine species, particularly PC (18:0/18:1), which in turn modulates skeletal muscle fatty acid uptake via PPARα activation, we propose a novel hypothesis linking circadian regulation of hepatic PPARβ/δ to systemic metabolic homeostasis. This hypothesis suggests that disruptions in the diurnal activity of hepatic PPARβ/δ may impair the secretion of lipid mediators necessary for optimal muscle fatty acid oxidation, thereby contributing to dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and progression of NAFLD. By targeting the circadian modulation of hepatic PPARβ/δ, it may be possible to restore inter-organ lipid communication and provide a chronotherapeutic strategy for metabolic disorders.
